blocks.en: "For the word of God is living and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword…"
blocks.es_reference: «Porque la palabra de Dios es viva y eficaz, y más penetrante que toda espada de dos filos…»

blocks.en: Unit Scripture: "For the word of God is living and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the division of soul and spirit, and of joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart." — Hebrews 4:12 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: Escritura de la Unidad: «Porque la palabra de Dios es viva y eficaz, y más penetrante que toda espada de dos filos; y penetra hasta partir el alma y el espíritu, y las coyunturas y tuétanos, y discierne los pensamientos y las intenciones del corazón». — Hebreos 4:12 (RVG)

blocks.en: Orientation: The Word That Reads the Reader
blocks.es_reference: Orientación: La Palabra que lee al lector

blocks.en: You have arrived at the last unit. Eleven units, two alphabets, a dozen Greek and Hebrew words, the Strong's number system, the textual story from Sinai to your phone. You came in not able to read either alphabet. You are leaving able to read both, look up any word in any verse, and trace it through every other place it appears in the Bible. The journey is almost over. One assignment stands between you and the certificate of completion: your first real word study.
blocks.es_reference: Has llegado a la última unidad. Once unidades, dos alfabetos, una docena de palabras griegas y hebreas, el sistema de números de Strong, la historia textual desde el Sinaí hasta tu teléfono. Entraste sin poder leer ninguno de los alfabetos. Te vas pudiendo leer ambos, buscar cualquier palabra en cualquier versículo, y rastrearla a través de cada otro lugar donde aparece en la Biblia. El viaje está casi terminado. Una tarea se interpone entre tú y el certificado de finalización: tu primer estudio real de palabras.

blocks.en: Our unit scripture is Hebrews 4:12. The Greek opens zôn gar ho logos tou theou, "for living is the word of God." Notice the verse. The author of Hebrews does not say the Word of God contains living truth. He says the Word is living. The Greek word is zôn (Strong's G2198, the present active participle of zaô), and it means the same thing in Greek that it means in English: alive, breathing, animate. The Word of God is not a museum exhibit; Scripture itself is alive and active, and in it we meet the living Christ, of whom all Scripture speaks. And the next Greek word, energês (Strong's G1756), carries the sense of actively working, in operation, producing effect — it is related to the idea behind our English word "energy," though the English word is not proof of the Greek one; energês earns its meaning from how Hebrews and other Greek writers actually use it, not from its English descendant. The Word does not sit on the shelf waiting to be admired. It works. It pierces. It divides. It discerns. The Word reads the reader.
blocks.es_reference: Nuestra escritura es Hebreos 4:12. El griego abre zôn gar ho logos tou theou, «pues vive la palabra de Dios». Nota el versículo. El autor de Hebreos no dice que la Palabra de Dios contiene verdad viva. Dice que la Palabra es viva. La palabra griega es zôn (número de Strong G2198, el participio presente activo de zaô), y significa lo mismo en griego que en español: viva, respirante, animada. La Palabra de Dios no es una exhibición de museo; la Escritura misma está viva y activa, y en ella nos encontramos con el Cristo vivo, de quien habla toda la Escritura. Y la siguiente palabra griega, energês (número de Strong G1756), lleva el sentido de trabajar activamente, en operación, produciendo efecto — se relaciona con la idea detrás de la palabra energía, aunque esa palabra no es prueba del significado griego; energês obtiene su significado de cómo la usan realmente Hebreos y otros escritores griegos, no de su descendiente moderna. La Palabra no se queda en el estante esperando a ser admirada. Trabaja. Penetra. Divide. Discierne. La Palabra lee al lector.

blocks.en: You did not study the Word for eleven weeks. The Word studied you. That is the secret of every honest course in Scripture.
blocks.es_reference: No estudiaste la Palabra durante once semanas. La Palabra te estudió a ti. Ese es el secreto de todo curso honesto en las Escrituras.

blocks.en: What this unit will do
blocks.es_reference: Lo que hará esta unidad

blocks.en: Unit 11 has one main job: walk you through a complete word study from start to finish, using one Greek word as the worked example, so that you have a model in your hand for the capstone assignment you will turn in to Wayne. Section I sets out the six-step workflow you saw at the end of Unit 10. Section II is the worked example — a full word study of euangelion, the Greek word for "gospel." Section III spells out your capstone assignment in detail. Section IV looks back over the whole eleven-unit course. Section V is the closing charge. After you pass the examination, the certificate of completion unlocks. You will have earned it.
blocks.es_reference: La Unidad 11 tiene un trabajo principal: guiarte a través de un estudio de palabras completo de principio a fin, usando una palabra griega como ejemplo, para que tengas un modelo en mano para la tarea final que entregarás a Wayne. La Sección I expone el flujo de trabajo de seis pasos que viste al final de la Unidad 10. La Sección II es el ejemplo trabajado — un estudio completo de palabras de euangelion, la palabra griega para «evangelio». La Sección III detalla tu tarea final. La Sección IV mira atrás sobre todo el curso de once unidades. La Sección V es la última exhortación. Después de que apruebes el examen, el certificado de finalización se desbloqueará. Lo habrás ganado.

blocks.en: I. The Anatomy of a Word Study — Six Steps
blocks.es_reference: I. La anatomía de un estudio de palabras — Seis pasos

blocks.en: A complete word study has six steps. None of them is hard. All of them require honest attention. Together they take about forty-five minutes for the kind of study Wayne will ask you to turn in for this capstone. Here is the workflow, with the verbs that actually do the work in each step.
blocks.es_reference: Un estudio de palabras completo tiene seis pasos. Ninguno es difícil. Todos requieren atención honesta. Juntos toman unos cuarenta y cinco minutos para el tipo de estudio que Wayne te pedirá entregar para este remate. Aquí está el flujo de trabajo, con los verbos que en realidad hacen el trabajo en cada paso.

blocks.en: Step 1: CHOOSE. Pick a verse, then pick the key word in the verse you want to investigate. Choose a meaningful word — usually a noun or verb that carries the doctrinal weight of the verse. Avoid articles, prepositions, and conjunctions ("the," "and," "of") — they rarely repay study.
blocks.es_reference: Paso 1: ELIGE. Elige un versículo, luego elige la palabra clave del versículo que quieres investigar. Elige una palabra significativa — usualmente un sustantivo o verbo que cargue el peso doctrinal del versículo. Evita artículos, preposiciones, y conjunciones («el», «y», «de») — rara vez recompensan el estudio.

blocks.en: Step 2: LOOK UP. Find the Strong's number for that English word in that verse. Use Blue Letter Bible, Bible Hub, or any other Strong's-keyed tool you learned in Unit 10. The number unlocks everything downstream.
blocks.es_reference: Paso 2: BUSCA. Encuentra el número de Strong para esa palabra en ese versículo. Usa Blue Letter Bible, Bible Hub, o cualquier otra herramienta numerada a Strong que aprendiste en la Unidad 10. El número desbloquea todo lo demás.

blocks.en: Step 3: READ. Read the lexicon entry for the Greek or Hebrew word. Start with Strong's own brief definition. Then read Thayer's (Greek) or Brown-Driver-Briggs (Hebrew) for the longer scholarly entry. Note the word's range of meanings, its etymology, and any cross-language notes.
blocks.es_reference: Paso 3: LEE. Lee la entrada del lexicón para la palabra griega o hebrea. Empieza con la definición breve de Strong. Luego lee Thayer (griego) o Brown-Driver-Briggs (hebreo) para la entrada erudita más larga. Nota el rango de significados de la palabra, su etimología, y cualquier nota entre idiomas.

blocks.en: Step 4: TRACE. Click "every occurrence" of the same Strong's number. Read the verse list. For a common word (like agapê) the list is long; sample five to ten representative verses across different books. For a rare word the list is short; read every occurrence.
blocks.es_reference: Paso 4: RASTREA. Haz clic en «cada ocurrencia» del mismo número de Strong. Lee la lista de versículos. Para una palabra común (como agapê) la lista es larga; muestrea de cinco a diez versículos representativos a través de diferentes libros. Para una palabra rara la lista es corta; lee cada ocurrencia.

blocks.en: Step 5: COMPARE. If your word is Greek and the New Testament author is quoting or alluding to the Old Testament, find the Hebrew word it translates in the Septuagint. (Bible Hub has an LXX search; Blue Letter Bible's NT verse-list often points to the OT source.) Many New Testament words carry centuries of Hebrew freight.
blocks.es_reference: Paso 5: COMPARA. Si tu palabra es griega y el autor del Nuevo Testamento está citando o aludiendo al Antiguo Testamento, encuentra la palabra hebrea que traduce en la Septuaginta. (Bible Hub tiene una búsqueda LXX; la lista de versículos del NT en Blue Letter Bible a menudo apunta a la fuente del AT.) Muchas palabras del Nuevo Testamento cargan siglos de carga hebrea.

blocks.en: Step 6: RETURN. Go back to your original verse and reread it. The same English text now has new depth. Write your findings in a few hundred words. Do not show off; show insight. The goal is not to display learning. The goal is to feed the church.
blocks.es_reference: Paso 6: REGRESA. Vuelve a tu versículo original y reléelo. El mismo texto castellano ahora tiene nueva profundidad. Escribe tus hallazgos en unos pocos cientos de palabras. No te luzcas; muestra perspicacia. La meta no es exhibir aprendizaje. La meta es alimentar a la iglesia.

blocks.en: That last sentence is the difference between a word study that builds the Body and a word study that builds the student. Wayne has read thousands of word studies over his teaching years. The good ones change the way the writer reads Scripture. The great ones change the way the writer's congregation reads Scripture. As you do your capstone, remember whom you are studying for.
blocks.es_reference: Esa última oración es la diferencia entre un estudio de palabras que edifica el Cuerpo y un estudio de palabras que edifica al estudiante. Wayne ha leído miles de estudios de palabras en sus años de enseñanza. Los buenos cambian la manera en que el escritor lee las Escrituras. Los grandes cambian la manera en que la congregación del escritor lee las Escrituras. Mientras haces tu remate, recuerda para quién estás estudiando.

blocks.en: II. A Worked Example: EUANGELION (ευαγγελιον) — Gospel
blocks.es_reference: II. Un ejemplo trabajado: EUANGELION (ευαγγελιον) — Evangelio

blocks.en: good news, good announcement; specifically the message of salvation through Jesus Christ
blocks.es_reference: buenas nuevas, buena proclamación; específicamente el mensaje de salvación a través de Jesucristo

blocks.en: Watch what a complete word study looks like. Here is one from start to finish, applying all six steps to a single Greek word. You will follow the same pattern for your capstone.
blocks.es_reference: Observa cómo se ve un estudio de palabras completo. Aquí hay uno de principio a fin, aplicando los seis pasos a una sola palabra griega. Seguirás el mismo patrón para tu remate.

blocks.en: Step 1 (CHOOSE): The verse and the word
blocks.es_reference: Paso 1 (ELIGE): El versículo y la palabra

blocks.en: We return to Romans 1:16 from Unit 9: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation." We pick the English word "gospel" — the doctrinal heart of the verse. Without "gospel" the sentence collapses.
blocks.es_reference: Volvemos a Romanos 1:16 de la Unidad 9: «Porque no me avergüenzo del evangelio de Cristo, porque es el poder de Dios para salvación». Elegimos la palabra «evangelio» — el corazón doctrinal del versículo. Sin «evangelio» la oración se desploma.

blocks.en: Step 2 (LOOK UP): The Strong's number
blocks.es_reference: Paso 2 (BUSCA): El número de Strong

blocks.en: Open Bible Hub or Blue Letter Bible. Find Romans 1:16. Tap or hover over "gospel." The Strong's number appears: G2098. The Greek word is euangelion. Three seconds of work and the bridge is built.
blocks.es_reference: Abre Bible Hub o Blue Letter Bible. Encuentra Romanos 1:16. Toca o pasa el cursor sobre «gospel» (la palabra para evangelio en inglés, ya que la mayoría de las herramientas todavía están en inglés primero). Aparece el número de Strong: G2098. La palabra griega es euangelion. Tres segundos de trabajo y el puente está construido.

blocks.en: Step 3 (READ): The lexicon
blocks.es_reference: Paso 3 (LEE): El lexicón

blocks.en: Strong's brief entry says: "a good message, good news." Thayer's longer entry adds the etymology: eu- ("good") + angelion ("a message, announcement") from angelos (the word that gives us "angel," literally a messenger). So euangelion is etymologically "the good announcement." Thayer continues: in classical Greek before the New Testament, the word was used for a public proclamation of victory — especially the announcement that a military campaign had been won, or that a new emperor had ascended the throne. It was a herald's word. When a Roman emperor was born, the Roman world received the news as euangelion. When that emperor won a battle, Rome celebrated with euangelion. The word in the first century had imperial weight.
blocks.es_reference: La entrada breve de Strong dice: «un buen mensaje, buenas nuevas». La entrada más larga de Thayer agrega la etimología: eu- («bueno») + angelion («un mensaje, anuncio») de angelos (la palabra que nos da «ángel», literalmente un mensajero). Así que euangelion es etimológicamente «el buen anuncio». Thayer continúa: en el griego clásico antes del Nuevo Testamento, la palabra se usaba para una proclamación pública de victoria — especialmente el anuncio de que una campaña militar había sido ganada, o que un nuevo emperador había ascendido al trono. Era una palabra de heraldo. Cuando un emperador romano nacía, el mundo romano recibía la noticia como euangelion. Cuando ese emperador ganaba una batalla, Roma celebraba con euangelion. La palabra en el primer siglo tenía peso imperial.

blocks.en: Step 4 (TRACE): Every occurrence in the New Testament
blocks.es_reference: Paso 4 (RASTREA): Cada ocurrencia en el Nuevo Testamento

blocks.en: Strong's number G2098 appears 76 times in the Greek New Testament. The verb form euangelizô (G2097, "to announce good news") appears another 54 times. Together over 130 occurrences. The word is dense in Paul (60+ uses), prominent in the Synoptic Gospels (Matthew and Mark especially), and culminates in Revelation 14:6 where an angel proclaims the "everlasting euangelion." Sample five strategic verses:
blocks.es_reference: El número de Strong G2098 aparece 76 veces en el Nuevo Testamento griego. La forma verbal euangelizô (G2097, «anunciar buenas nuevas») aparece otras 54 veces. Juntos más de 130 ocurrencias. La palabra es densa en Pablo (60+ usos), prominente en los Evangelios Sinópticos (Mateo y Marcos especialmente), y culmina en Apocalipsis 14:6 donde un ángel proclama el «evangelio eterno» (euangelion). Muestrea cinco versículos estratégicos:

blocks.en: <th>Verse</th><th>What it tells us about euangelion</th>
blocks.es_reference: <th>Versículo</th><th>Lo que nos dice sobre euangelion</th>

blocks.en: Mark 1:1"The beginning of the euangelion of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." The opening word of the second Gospel. The gospel BEGINS here; everything before was preparation.
blocks.es_reference: Marcos 1:1«Principio del euangelion de Jesucristo, Hijo de Dios». La palabra inicial del segundo Evangelio. El evangelio EMPIEZA aquí; todo lo anterior fue preparación.

blocks.en: Romans 1:1Paul calls himself "separated unto the euangelion of God." His whole life is now defined by carrying one piece of news.
blocks.es_reference: Romanos 1:1Pablo se llama «apartado para el euangelion de Dios». Toda su vida ahora está definida por llevar una sola noticia.

blocks.en: 1 Corinthians 15:1–4Paul's clearest summary: the euangelion is "Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; and that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day." Death, burial, resurrection. Three historical events.
blocks.es_reference: 1 Corintios 15:1–4El resumen más claro de Pablo: el euangelion es «Cristo murió por nuestros pecados conforme a las Escrituras; y que fue sepultado, y que resucitó al tercer día». Muerte, sepultura, resurrección. Tres eventos históricos.

blocks.en: Galatians 1:8–9Paul anathematizes anyone preaching a different euangelion — not different doctrines in general, but a different gospel. The message is so specific that it can be falsified.
blocks.es_reference: Gálatas 1:8–9Pablo anatematiza a cualquiera que predique un euangelion diferente — no diferentes doctrinas en general, sino un evangelio diferente. El mensaje es tan específico que puede ser falsificado.

blocks.en: Revelation 14:6The "everlasting euangelion" preached to every nation. The same good news, now reaching the last island and the last language. The story closes with the word that opened.
blocks.es_reference: Apocalipsis 14:6El «euangelion eterno» predicado a toda nación. La misma buena noticia, ahora llegando a la última isla y al último idioma. La historia se cierra con la palabra que la abrió.

blocks.en: Step 5 (COMPARE): The Old Testament Hebrew background
blocks.es_reference: Paso 5 (COMPARA): El trasfondo hebreo del Antiguo Testamento

blocks.en: This is where word study often pays its biggest dividend. Euangelion did not appear from nowhere in the first century. The Septuagint (the Greek Old Testament we met in Unit 2) had used the verb form euangelizô in two places that the New Testament writers all knew by heart. Both passages translate the Hebrew verb basar (H1319), "to announce good news."
blocks.es_reference: Aquí es donde el estudio de palabras a menudo paga su mayor dividendo. Euangelion no apareció de la nada en el primer siglo. La Septuaginta (el Antiguo Testamento griego que conocimos en la Unidad 2) había usado la forma verbal euangelizô en dos lugares que todos los escritores del Nuevo Testamento conocían de memoria. Ambos pasajes traducen el verbo hebreo basar (H1319), «anunciar buenas nuevas».

blocks.en: Isaiah 52:7: "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!" The Hebrew basar stands behind "bringeth good tidings." The LXX renders it euangelizomenou. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 10:15 to argue that gospel preaching is the prophesied work of the Messiah's heralds. The runners over the mountains in Isaiah's vision are the apostles, the evangelists, every Christian who has ever taken the news to a neighbor.
blocks.es_reference: Isaías 52:7: «¡Cuán hermosos son sobre los montes los pies del que trae buenas nuevas, del que publica paz, del que trae nuevas del bien, del que publica salvación, del que dice a Sión: Tu Dios reina!» El hebreo basar está detrás de «trae buenas nuevas». La LXX lo traduce euangelizomenou. Pablo cita este versículo en Romanos 10:15 para argumentar que la predicación del evangelio es la obra profetizada de los heraldos del Mesías. Los corredores sobre los montes en la visión de Isaías son los apóstoles, los evangelistas, cada cristiano que ha llevado alguna vez la noticia a un vecino.

blocks.en: Isaiah 61:1: "The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me; because the Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek." Hebrew basar again. LXX euangelisasthai. And Jesus reads this very verse at His hometown synagogue in Luke 4:18, applies it to Himself, and announces that the prophecy is now fulfilled. The Old Testament basar and the New Testament euangelion are the same word in two languages. Seven hundred years of Hebrew prophetic anticipation flows into one Greek noun.
blocks.es_reference: Isaías 61:1: «El Espíritu del Señor Dios está sobre mí, porque me ha ungido el Señor; me ha enviado a predicar buenas nuevas a los mansos». Hebreo basar de nuevo. LXX euangelisasthai. Y Jesús lee este mismo versículo en la sinagoga de su pueblo natal en Lucas 4:18, lo aplica a Sí mismo, y anuncia que la profecía ahora se cumple. El basar del Antiguo Testamento y el euangelion del Nuevo Testamento son la misma palabra en dos idiomas. Setecientos años de anticipación profética hebrea fluyen en un sustantivo griego.

blocks.en: Step 6 (RETURN): Rereading Romans 1:16
blocks.es_reference: Paso 6 (REGRESA): Releyendo Romanos 1:16

blocks.en: Now reread the verse: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation." Here is what the word now carries. The Roman world had its own euangelion — the proclamation of imperial victory, the announcement of Caesar's birthday, the news of a new emperor on the throne. Paul writes this letter to Rome, the imperial capital, and uses the same word for a rival announcement: the news that a different Lord (kyrios — remember Unit 9?) has been enthroned. The cross looked like defeat. The resurrection turned it into euangelion. And Paul claims this rival announcement is the power of God unto salvation. It does what Caesar's euangelion never did. It saves. The Greek word is doing imperial-versus-Christ work in the very verse Luther saw the Reformation in. Romans 1:16 is more layered than the English alone reveals. Euangelion opens those layers.
blocks.es_reference: Ahora relee el versículo: «Porque no me avergüenzo del evangelio de Cristo, porque es el poder de Dios para salvación». Aquí está lo que la palabra ahora carga. El mundo romano tenía su propio euangelion — la proclamación de la victoria imperial, el anuncio del cumpleaños del César, las noticias de un nuevo emperador en el trono. Pablo escribe esta carta a Roma, la capital imperial, y usa la misma palabra para un anuncio rival: las nuevas de que un Señor diferente (kyrios — ¿recuerdas la Unidad 9?) ha sido entronizado. La cruz parecía una derrota. La resurrección la convirtió en euangelion. Y Pablo afirma que este anuncio rival es el poder de Dios para salvación. Hace lo que el euangelion del César nunca hizo. Salva. La palabra griega está haciendo trabajo imperial-versus-Cristo en el mismo versículo donde Lutero vio la Reforma. Romanos 1:16 es más en capas de lo que el español solo revela. Euangelion abre esas capas.

blocks.en: In Caesar's Rome, the gospel was a proclamation of imperial victory. Paul wrote to Rome that there was a different Victor and a different victory. The Greek word euangelion carries the entire collision.
blocks.es_reference: En la Roma del César, el evangelio era una proclamación de victoria imperial. Pablo escribió a Roma que había un Vencedor diferente y una victoria diferente. La palabra griega euangelion carga toda la colisión.

blocks.en: English derivatives
blocks.es_reference: Derivados en español

blocks.en: The word family is generous in English. Evangel is an archaic English word for the gospel itself. An evangelist is one who announces it. Evangelism is the activity. Evangelical is the adjective for a movement committed to it. The four Gospels — Matthew, Mark, Luke, John — are literally "the four evangelia." Every time you say one of these English words, the Greek euangelion stands behind your mouth.
blocks.es_reference: La familia de palabras es generosa. Evangelio es la palabra inmediata. Un evangelista es quien lo anuncia. Evangelismo es la actividad. Evangélico es el adjetivo para un movimiento comprometido con él. Los cuatro Evangelios — Mateo, Marcos, Lucas, Juan — son literalmente «los cuatro evangelia». Cada vez que dices una de estas palabras castellanas, el griego euangelion está detrás de tu boca.

blocks.en: Length and shape of the worked example
blocks.es_reference: Longitud y forma del ejemplo trabajado

blocks.en: This worked example, in English, runs about 950 words across the six steps. A capstone word study in the 800-word range will be similar in shape. Notice the proportions: about 200 words on the lexicon and etymology, 300 words on tracing through the New Testament, 250 words on the Old Testament Hebrew background, and 200 words on the rereading of the original verse. Adjust these proportions according to your word, but keep all six steps represented.
blocks.es_reference: Este ejemplo trabajado, en español, corre alrededor de 950 palabras a través de los seis pasos. Un estudio de palabras de remate en el rango de 800 palabras será similar en forma. Nota las proporciones: cerca de 200 palabras sobre el lexicón y la etimología, 300 palabras rastreando a través del Nuevo Testamento, 250 palabras sobre el trasfondo hebreo del Antiguo Testamento, y 200 palabras sobre la relectura del versículo original. Ajusta estas proporciones según tu palabra, pero mantén los seis pasos representados.

blocks.en: III. Your Capstone Assignment
blocks.es_reference: III. Tu tarea de remate

blocks.en: Here is the assignment Wayne will receive from you.
blocks.es_reference: Aquí está la tarea que Wayne recibirá de ti.

blocks.en:
Capstone Word Study Assignment

Choose one Greek word from the New Testament. Strongly preferred: a word from Units 5 through 9 (logos, agapê, charis, pneuma, pistis, sôzô, dikaiosynê, kyrios, or any of the Hebrew words from Unit 5). Alternative: any other Greek or Hebrew word approved in advance by Wayne.

Write a word study of approximately 800 words covering all six steps:
1. The verse you chose and why you chose this word in it.
2. The Strong's number and the lexicon entry (Strong's + Thayer's or BDB).
3. The word's range of meaning and any notable etymology.
4. A trace across the New Testament (or OT) noting 5–10 representative occurrences.
5. The Old Testament Hebrew background, if applicable (find the LXX equivalent of any NT Greek word that translates a Hebrew word).
6. The rereading of your original verse with the word's full range now in view.

Submit by the deadline Wayne announces. Word count target: 750–900 words.
blocks.es_reference:
Tarea de estudio de palabras de remate

Elige una palabra griega del Nuevo Testamento. Fuertemente preferido: una palabra de las Unidades 5 a 9 (logos, agapê, charis, pneuma, pistis, sôzô, dikaiosynê, kyrios, o cualquiera de las palabras hebreas de la Unidad 5). Alternativa: cualquier otra palabra griega o hebrea aprobada de antemano por Wayne.

Escribe un estudio de palabras de aproximadamente 800 palabras cubriendo los seis pasos:
1. El versículo que elegiste y por qué elegiste esta palabra en él.
2. El número de Strong y la entrada del lexicón (Strong + Thayer o BDB).
3. El rango de significado de la palabra y cualquier etimología notable.
4. Un rastreo a través del Nuevo Testamento (o AT) notando 5–10 ocurrencias representativas.
5. El trasfondo hebreo del Antiguo Testamento, si aplica (encuentra el equivalente LXX de cualquier palabra griega del NT que traduzca una palabra hebrea).
6. La relectura de tu versículo original con el rango completo de la palabra ahora a la vista.

Entrega antes de la fecha límite que Wayne anuncie. Meta de conteo de palabras: 750–900 palabras.

blocks.en: Practical tips
blocks.es_reference: Consejos prácticos

blocks.en: Pick a word you actually care about. A word study you do because you want to understand something deeply about Christ or the Christian life will be readable. A word study you do because the assignment requires it will sound mechanical. Wayne can tell the difference within two paragraphs.
blocks.es_reference: Elige una palabra que realmente te importe. Un estudio de palabras que hagas porque quieres entender algo profundamente sobre Cristo o la vida cristiana será legible. Un estudio de palabras que hagas porque la tarea lo requiere sonará mecánico. Wayne puede notar la diferencia dentro de dos párrafos.

blocks.en: Use Blue Letter Bible (free app or website) as your primary tool. Use Bible Hub for the interlinear view if you want to see grammatical parsing. If you have access to Logos or e-Sword, fine, but you do not need them. Free tools are sufficient for this assignment.
blocks.es_reference: Usa Blue Letter Bible (aplicación o sitio web gratuito) como tu herramienta principal. Usa Bible Hub para la vista interlineal si quieres ver el análisis gramatical. Si tienes acceso a Logos o e-Sword, bien, pero no los necesitas. Las herramientas gratuitas son suficientes para esta tarea.

blocks.en: Avoid the three pitfalls from Unit 10. No root fallacy. Do not preach that the church is "dynamite." No illegitimate totality transfer. Let the context of your specific verse discipline which meaning of the word's range is actually in play. No "deeper meaning" trap. Strong's enriches the verse; it almost never overturns the English translation.
blocks.es_reference: Evita las tres trampas de la Unidad 10. Sin falacia de la raíz. No prediques que la iglesia es «dinamita». Sin transferencia ilegítima de totalidad. Deja que el contexto de tu versículo específico discipline cuál significado del rango de la palabra está realmente en juego. Sin trampa del «significado más profundo». Strong enriquece el versículo; casi nunca revierte la traducción.

blocks.en: Cite your sources. When you quote Strong's or Thayer's, say so. When you quote a verse, give the reference. The point is not to display your sources; the point is to make your reasoning checkable. Be a Berean for your reader the way you have been a Berean for Paul.
blocks.es_reference: Cita tus fuentes. Cuando cites a Strong o Thayer, dilo. Cuando cites un versículo, da la referencia. El punto no es exhibir tus fuentes; el punto es hacer tu razonamiento verificable. Sé un bereano para tu lector de la manera que has sido un bereano para Pablo.

blocks.en: IV. Looking Back: The Eleven-Unit Journey
blocks.es_reference: IV. Mirando atrás: El viaje de once unidades

blocks.en: You came in eleven units ago with an English Bible and a curiosity. You are leaving with two alphabets, a dictionary of fundamental Greek and Hebrew vocabulary, the Strong's number system, and a workflow for opening any word in Scripture. Look at the road behind you:
blocks.es_reference: Entraste hace once unidades con una Biblia castellana y una curiosidad. Te vas con dos alfabetos, un diccionario de vocabulario fundamental griego y hebreo, el sistema de números de Strong, y un flujo de trabajo para abrir cualquier palabra en la Escritura. Mira el camino atrás de ti:

blocks.en: <th>Unit</th><th>What you gained</th>
blocks.es_reference: <th>Unidad</th><th>Lo que ganaste</th>

blocks.en: 1–2The textual story: how the Bible came from God's breath to your hand, through Hebrew scribes, Greek copyists, Jerome's Latin, Wycliffe and Tyndale's English, the Reformation, and modern translations like NKJV and RVG.
blocks.es_reference: 1–2La historia textual: cómo la Biblia vino del aliento de Dios a tu mano, a través de escribas hebreos, copistas griegos, el latín de Jerónimo, el inglés de Wycliffe y Tyndale, la Reforma, y traducciones modernas como NKJV y RVG.

blocks.en: 3–4The Hebrew alphabet: 22 consonants, the Aleph-Tav arc, the right-to-left reading direction, and the first Hebrew words you ever read.
blocks.es_reference: 3–4El alfabeto hebreo: 22 consonantes, el arco Aleph-Tav, la dirección de lectura de derecha a izquierda, y las primeras palabras hebreas que leíste.

blocks.en: 5Hebrew word treasures: hesed, shalom, ruach, dabar — the great covenant vocabulary of the Old Testament.
blocks.es_reference: 5Tesoros de palabras hebreas: hesed, shalom, ruach, dabar — el gran vocabulario del pacto del Antiguo Testamento.

blocks.en: 6–7The Greek alphabet: 24 letters, Alpha to Omega, the false-friend warnings (Nu, Rho, Chi), and reading John 1:1 in Greek for the first time.
blocks.es_reference: 6–7El alfabeto griego: 24 letras, de Alfa a Omega, las advertencias de falsos amigos (Nu, Rho, Ji), y leer Juan 1:1 en griego por primera vez.

blocks.en: 8Four Greek words from John: Logos, agapê, charis, pneuma. The Person revealed, the love that sent Him, the grace He brings, the Spirit He gives.
blocks.es_reference: 8Cuatro palabras griegas de Juan: Logos, agapê, charis, pneuma. La Persona revelada, el amor que lo envió, la gracia que trae, el Espíritu que da.

blocks.en: 9Four Greek words from Romans: pistis, sôzô, dikaiosynê, kyrios. The faith that receives Him, the salvation He works, the righteousness He grants, the Lordship He claims. Luther's verse opened.
blocks.es_reference: 9Cuatro palabras griegas de Romanos: pistis, sôzô, dikaiosynê, kyrios. La fe que lo recibe, la salvación que obra, la justicia que concede, el Señorío que reclama. El versículo de Lutero abierto.

blocks.en: 10Strong's numbers in three forms — paper, phone, internet. The bridge tool that puts every Hebrew and Greek word into your hand.
blocks.es_reference: 10Los números de Strong en tres formas — papel, teléfono, internet. La herramienta del puente que pone cada palabra hebrea y griega en tu mano.

blocks.en: 11Your first complete word study. The tool meets the workman. The course produces fruit.
blocks.es_reference: 11Tu primer estudio de palabras completo. La herramienta encuentra al obrero. El curso produce fruto.

blocks.en: The Thesis of This Course
blocks.es_reference: La Tesis de Este Curso

blocks.en: The Bible is one Book, by one Author, on one Theme, about one Hero. Every chapter of Scripture, every paragraph, every sentence, ultimately points to Christ. Eleven units later, that thesis is no longer abstract. You have traced it in the Hebrew Aleph-Tav (Christ the First and Last), in the Greek Alpha-Omega (the same title in the language of Revelation), in Logos (the Word made flesh), in agapê (the love that drove Him to the cross), in charis (the gift He brings), in pneuma (the Spirit He sends), in pistis (the faith that receives Him), in sôzô (the salvation He works), in dikaiosynê (the righteousness He grants), and in kyrios (the Lordship He claims). One Hero. Many languages. Every word in this course was a window onto His face.
blocks.es_reference: La Biblia es un Libro, por un Autor, sobre un Tema, acerca de un Héroe. Cada capítulo de la Escritura, cada párrafo, cada oración, en última instancia apunta a Cristo. Once unidades después, esa tesis ya no es abstracta. La has rastreado en el Aleph-Tav hebreo (Cristo el Primero y el Último), en el Alfa-Omega griego (el mismo título en el idioma del Apocalipsis), en Logos (el Verbo hecho carne), en agapê (el amor que lo llevó a la cruz), en charis (el regalo que trae), en pneuma (el Espíritu que envía), en pistis (la fe que lo recibe), en sôzô (la salvación que obra), en dikaiosynê (la justicia que concede), y en kyrios (el Señorío que reclama). Un Héroe. Muchos idiomas. Cada palabra en este curso fue una ventana sobre Su rostro.

blocks.en: Eleven units, two alphabets, a dozen words, one Hero. The whole course was about Him.
blocks.es_reference: Once unidades, dos alfabetos, una docena de palabras, un Héroe. Todo el curso fue acerca de Él.

blocks.en: V. The Closing Charge
blocks.es_reference: V. La última exhortación

blocks.en: Three things, before you go.
blocks.es_reference: Tres cosas, antes de irte.

blocks.en: First, keep doing this. A workman who studies once is not a workman. A workman is the man who comes back to the workbench every morning. Make Strong's lookup a part of your daily Bible reading from now on. Tap a word every day. Read one lexicon entry. Trace one Strong's number. Sermon preparation, daily devotions, Sunday-school lessons, family worship — all of them are better when one Greek or Hebrew word per study is opened to its depth. You have the tools. Use them.
blocks.es_reference: Primero, sigue haciendo esto. Un obrero que estudia una vez no es un obrero. Un obrero es el hombre que vuelve al banco de trabajo cada mañana. Haz de la búsqueda Strong parte de tu lectura bíblica diaria de ahora en adelante. Toca una palabra cada día. Lee una entrada del lexicón. Rastrea un número de Strong. Preparación de sermones, devocionales diarios, lecciones de escuela dominical, adoración familiar — todos son mejores cuando una palabra griega o hebrea por estudio se abre a su profundidad. Tienes las herramientas. Úsalas.

blocks.en: Second, do not let the tools replace the Word. Hebrews 4:12 said the Word of God is living and energês — active, working, in operation. Strong's is a screwdriver. The Word is a sword. The screwdriver helps you open and adjust the sword's handle; it does not replace the blade. Read your English or Spanish Bible every day. Pray your way through psalms. Let the Word read you. The original-language work serves the daily reading; it does not displace it.
blocks.es_reference: Segundo, no dejes que las herramientas reemplacen la Palabra. Hebreos 4:12 dijo que la Palabra de Dios es viva y energês — activa, trabajando, en operación. Strong es un destornillador. La Palabra es una espada. El destornillador te ayuda a abrir y ajustar el mango de la espada; no reemplaza la hoja. Lee tu Biblia castellana o inglesa cada día. Ora a través de los salmos. Deja que la Palabra te lea. El trabajo en lengua original sirve a la lectura diaria; no la desplaza.

blocks.en: Third, hand this on. A pastor or layperson who can open a Greek word that his congregation has never seen opened is a pastor of unusual value to his people. Teach what you have learned. Show one church member how to use Blue Letter Bible. Show one new convert what agapê means. Share one Strong's lookup at the next prayer meeting. The seminary went into the hand of the layman in 1890. Your job is to keep handing it on.
blocks.es_reference: Tercero, transmite esto. Un pastor o laico que puede abrir una palabra griega que su congregación nunca ha visto abierta es un pastor de valor inusual para su gente. Enseña lo que has aprendido. Muestra a un miembro de la iglesia cómo usar Blue Letter Bible. Muestra a un nuevo convertido qué significa agapê. Comparte una búsqueda Strong en la próxima reunión de oración. El seminario pasó a la mano del laico en 1890. Tu trabajo es seguir pasándolo.

blocks.en: You did not come to seminary to know more than your neighbor. You came to feed the Body of Christ. Take what you have been given and feed the sheep.
blocks.es_reference: No viniste al seminario para saber más que tu vecino. Viniste para alimentar al Cuerpo de Cristo. Toma lo que se te ha dado y alimenta a las ovejas.

blocks.en: And one last word
blocks.es_reference: Y una última palabra

blocks.en: Wayne began this course years ago out of a conviction that biblical languages do not belong to the academic class. They belong to the church. They are the inheritance of every believer who is willing to learn. This course is, in part, his gift of that inheritance to you. When you sit in the next prayer meeting and someone reads Romans 1:16 aloud, and you hear euangelion behind the English word "gospel," and the verse opens into Caesar-versus-Christ in a way it never did before — you have received what Wayne has spent his life trying to pass on. The candle is in your hand now. Carry it.
blocks.es_reference: Wayne comenzó este curso hace años por convicción de que las lenguas bíblicas no pertenecen a la clase académica. Pertenecen a la iglesia. Son la herencia de cada creyente que esté dispuesto a aprender. Este curso es, en parte, su regalo de esa herencia para ti. Cuando estés sentado en la próxima reunión de oración y alguien lea Romanos 1:16 en voz alta, y oigas euangelion detrás de la palabra «evangelio», y el versículo se abra a César-versus-Cristo de una manera que nunca lo hizo antes — has recibido lo que Wayne ha pasado su vida tratando de transmitir. La vela está ahora en tu mano. Llévala.

blocks.en: Now sit the examination. Pass it. The certificate of completion is waiting on the other side. And then write your word study. Wayne will be glad to read it.
blocks.es_reference: Ahora toma el examen. Apruébalo. El certificado de finalización está esperando al otro lado. Y luego escribe tu estudio de palabras. Wayne se alegrará de leerlo.

blocks.en: 📚 Catalog / Catálogo
εὐαγγέλιον
euangelion
Strong's G2098

mc.stem: What are the six steps of a complete word study, in the correct order?
options: Pray, sing, fast, confess, partake, rest
Choose, look up, read, trace, compare, return
Translate, memorize, parse, conjugate, decline, recite
Read the verse five times in five different translations
mc.why: The six steps are: CHOOSE (a verse and a meaningful word), LOOK UP (the Strong's number), READ (the lexicon entry), TRACE (every other occurrence of the same Strong's number), COMPARE (the OT Hebrew background if applicable), RETURN (to the original verse for a deeper rereading). Together they take about forty-five minutes and produce a word study worth turning in.

mc.stem: In our unit scripture, Hebrews 4:12, the Greek word translated 'living' is zôn (Strong's G2198). What is its closest English meaning?
options: Memorized
Printed
Alive, breathing, animate — the present active participle of zaô (to live)
Translated
mc.why: Zôn is the present active participle of zaô, 'to live.' It means 'living' in the sense of 'currently alive, breathing, animate.' The author of Hebrews is not saying the Word of God CONTAINS living truth; he is saying the Word IS alive. It is not a museum exhibit; it is a Person you meet and a sword that pierces. Strong's G2198 unlocks this immediately.

mc.stem: In Hebrews 4:12, the Greek word translated 'powerful' or 'effective' is energês (Strong's G1756). What English word derives from it?
options: Empty
Equator
Echo
Energy, energetic — actively working, in operation, producing effect
mc.why: Energês (G1756) is built from en- ('in') + ergon ('work'), literally 'in operation, at work.' English 'energy' comes directly from this Greek root. The Word of God is not just declared; it is at work, actively producing effect. Hebrews 4:12 says the Word pierces, divides, discerns — this is energês in action. The screwdriver of Strong's helps adjust the sword's handle; the blade itself is the Word.

mc.stem: What is the Greek word for 'gospel,' and what is its Strong's number?
options: euangelion, Strong's G2098
agapê, Strong's G26
logos, Strong's G3056
pneuma, Strong's G4151
mc.why: Euangelion (G2098) is the Greek noun for 'good news, good announcement.' It is built from eu- ('good') + angelion ('message, announcement') from angelos (the word that gives us 'angel,' literally 'messenger'). The verb form euangelizô (G2097) means 'to announce good news.' Together they appear over 130 times in the New Testament.

mc.stem: What is the etymological breakdown of the Greek word euangelion?
options: eu- ('good') + angelion ('message, announcement') = 'good announcement'
euros- ('European') + angel- ('angel') = 'European angel'
a-priv- ('not') + gelion ('cold') = 'not cold'
It has no etymology and is a randomly assigned word
mc.why: Euangelion = eu- ('good') + angelion ('a message, announcement'), with the angelion root tied to angelos ('messenger,' the same Greek word from which English 'angel' derives). Literally 'the good announcement.' Etymology is the first lexicon step in any Strong's-based word study.

mc.stem: In classical pre-Christian Greek, how was the word euangelion typically used?
options: As a generic word for 'letter' or 'postal communication'
As a public proclamation of victory — an announcement of military success or the ascension of a new emperor
As a curse word in Athenian politics
As a synonym for sacrifice to pagan gods
mc.why: In the first century, euangelion had imperial weight. It was a herald's word for the public proclamation that a military campaign had been won or that a new emperor had ascended the throne. When Paul writes from Rome that he is 'not ashamed of the euangelion of Christ,' he is using Caesar's vocabulary for a rival announcement: there is another Lord (kyrios), and the cross was His victory. The Greek word is doing imperial-versus-Christ work in Romans 1:16.

mc.stem: What Hebrew Old Testament word does euangelizô translate in the Septuagint, especially in the famous 'good news on the mountains' passage of Isaiah 52:7?
options: hesed (H2617, 'lovingkindness')
basar (H1319, 'to announce good news')
shalom (H7965, 'peace')
ruach (H7307, 'spirit')
mc.why: Hebrew basar (H1319) means 'to announce good news,' and the Septuagint regularly translates it with euangelizô. Isaiah 52:7 ('How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings') uses basar; the LXX renders euangelizomenou. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 10:15. Isaiah 61:1 ('preach good tidings unto the meek') is also basar; Jesus reads it in Luke 4:18 and applies it to Himself. The Old Testament basar and the New Testament euangelion are the same announcement in two languages.

mc.stem: In 1 Corinthians 15:1–4, Paul gives his clearest definition of the euangelion. According to that passage, the gospel is what?
options: A set of moral rules for Christian living
A philosophy of personal happiness
That Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures, was buried, and rose again the third day
A guide to social and political reform
mc.why: Paul's definition in 1 Corinthians 15:1–4 is the New Testament's clearest summary: the euangelion is the historical message that Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose the third day. Three historical events: death, burial, resurrection. The gospel is not a philosophy or a moral code; it is news about what happened in Jerusalem around AD 30. That is why it can be falsified, and that is why Paul anathematizes false versions of it in Galatians 1:8–9.

mc.stem: Which English words are derived from the Greek euangelion?
options: Equator, equilateral, equation
Echo, ecology, economy
Education, electron, election
Evangel, evangelist, evangelism, evangelical, and the names of the four Gospels themselves
mc.why: The Spanish 'evangelio' is immediate; English derivatives include 'evangel' (an archaic term for the gospel itself), 'evangelist' (one who proclaims it), 'evangelism' (the activity), 'evangelical' (the adjective for the movement committed to it). The four Gospels are literally 'the four evangelia.' Every time you say one of these words, the Greek euangelion stands behind your mouth.

mc.stem: According to the worked example in Unit 11, why does it matter that Paul wrote Romans (with its repeated use of euangelion) FROM and TO Rome, the imperial capital?
options: It does not matter; the location of writing is theologically irrelevant
Paul was using Caesar's own vocabulary (euangelion as imperial proclamation of victory) for a rival announcement — that a different Lord had won a different victory through the cross and resurrection
Paul wanted to make Roman emperors angry to provoke persecution
Romans was originally written in Latin, not Greek
mc.why: The worked example reveals a layer of Romans 1:16 the English alone cannot show. The Roman world had its own euangelion: imperial victories, the birth of a new emperor, the ascension of Caesar to the throne. Paul takes the exact same word and uses it for the news that a different Lord (kyrios — Unit 9 word) has been enthroned through the cross and resurrection. The cross looked like defeat; the resurrection turned it into euangelion. Paul's letter to the imperial capital is a deliberate rhetorical confrontation.

mc.stem: What is the approximate target length for the capstone word study assignment?
options: 3,000–5,000 words, the size of a doctoral dissertation
Two sentences
Approximately 800 words (range 750–900), covering all six steps
Exactly 144 words, one for each Hebrew letter
mc.why: The capstone target is approximately 800 words (750–900 range), covering all six steps of the word-study workflow: choose, look up, read, trace, compare, return. The worked example of euangelion in the unit runs about 950 words and gives you a template. Adjust proportions to your word, but make sure all six steps are represented.

mc.stem: Which Greek words from Units 8 and 9 are recommended (strongly preferred) options for your capstone word study?
options: Names of the twelve apostles only
Logos, agapê, charis, pneuma (Unit 8) and pistis, sôzô, dikaiosynê, kyrios (Unit 9) — plus the Hebrew word treasures from Unit 5
Place names only (Bethlehem, Galilee, Jerusalem)
Random words you have never seen before
mc.why: The strongly preferred capstone options are the words you have already met in Units 5–9: logos, agapê, charis, pneuma, pistis, sôzô, dikaiosynê, kyrios, plus the Hebrew word treasures from Unit 5 (hesed, shalom, ruach, dabar, etc.). You have already done some of the work in this course; the capstone deepens what you began. Alternative: any other Greek or Hebrew word approved in advance by Wayne.

mc.stem: What three pitfalls from Unit 10 must you avoid in your capstone word study?
options: Bad handwriting, late submission, missing citations
The root fallacy, the illegitimate totality transfer, and the 'deeper meaning' trap
Speaking Hebrew, speaking Greek, speaking Aramaic
Coffee stains, torn pages, lost flash drives
mc.why: The three classic pitfalls from Unit 10: the ROOT FALLACY (assuming an English derivative or etymological root tells you the 'real' meaning — e.g., 'dynamis means dynamite'); the ILLEGITIMATE TOTALITY TRANSFER (assuming every lexicon meaning is operative in every verse); the 'DEEPER MEANING' TRAP (assuming the Greek must overturn the English — usually it does not). Discipline yourself against all three in your capstone.

mc.stem: What is the recommended primary tool for performing your capstone word study?
options: Wikipedia
YouTube videos
Blue Letter Bible (free app or website) as primary, with Bible Hub for interlinear view as secondary
A printed 1611 King James Bible only
mc.why: Blue Letter Bible is the primary recommendation: free, available on iOS/Android/web, tap any word for instant Strong's number, lexicon, every occurrence, audio. Bible Hub adds the verse-by-verse interlinear with grammatical parsing. If you have Logos or e-Sword, fine; they are not necessary. The free tools are sufficient for the capstone and for a lifetime of word study afterward.

mc.stem: According to the closing charge of Unit 11, what is the main reason you came to seminary?
options: To prove yourself smarter than other people
To collect academic degrees
To feed the Body of Christ — to take what you have been given and feed the sheep
To win arguments on social media
mc.why: The closing charge: 'You did not come to seminary to know more than your neighbor. You came to feed the Body of Christ. Take what you have been given and feed the sheep.' The course was never about producing scholars who know Hebrew and Greek for its own sake. It was about producing workmen who feed congregations the bread that comes from the original Word. Strong's, lexicons, alphabets — all of them are tools that serve the people in the pews.

mc.stem: This course rests on a simple thesis about the entire Bible. What is it?
options: The Bible is many books, by many authors, on many themes, about many heroes
The Bible is mainly an instruction manual for moral living
The Bible is one Book, by one Author, on one Theme, about one Hero
The Bible should only be read by trained scholars
mc.why: The Bible is one Book, by one Author, on one Theme, about one Hero. Every chapter, every paragraph, every sentence ultimately points to Christ. The Language Appreciation course traced that thesis through Hebrew Aleph-Tav, Greek Alpha-Omega, Logos, agapê, charis, pneuma, pistis, sôzô, dikaiosynê, and kyrios. Every word in this course was a window onto His face.

mc.stem: What does Hebrews 4:12 say about the Word of God's effect on the reader?
options: It is dull and rusty, requiring patience to use
It is living and powerful, sharper than a two-edged sword, piercing soul and spirit, discerning the thoughts and intents of the heart
It is purely informational, like a textbook
It can only be understood by ordained clergy
mc.why: Hebrews 4:12 reveals the Word is alive (zôn), active (energês), and discerning (kritikos) — sharper than a two-edged sword (machaira), piercing through to soul and spirit, and reading the hearts of those who read it. You did not study the Word for eleven weeks; the Word studied you. That is the secret of every honest course in Scripture. The screwdriver of Strong's helps adjust the sword's handle, but the blade itself is the Word.

mc.stem: What metaphor does the closing charge use to compare Strong's tools to the Word of God itself?
options: Strong's is a microscope; the Word is a planet
Strong's is a phone; the Word is a letter
Strong's is a screwdriver; the Word is a sword. The screwdriver helps adjust the sword's handle but does not replace the blade
Strong's is a clock; the Word is the sun
mc.why: The closing metaphor: Strong's is a screwdriver, the Word is a sword. The screwdriver helps you open and adjust the sword's handle, but it does not replace the blade. Hebrews 4:12 names the Word as a two-edged sword that pierces; Strong's tools merely sharpen your grip on the handle. Do not let the workshop replace the battlefield. Read your Bible every day. Strong's serves daily reading; it does not displace it.

mc.stem: Roughly how many total occurrences do euangelion (G2098) and euangelizô (G2097) combined have in the Greek New Testament?
options: Fewer than 10
Over 130 occurrences (76 noun + 54 verb forms)
Exactly 7
Over 5,000
mc.why: Euangelion (G2098, the noun 'good news') appears 76 times in the NT. Euangelizô (G2097, the verb 'to announce good news') appears 54 times. Together over 130 occurrences. The word family is dense in Paul (60+ uses), prominent in Matthew and Mark, and culminates in Revelation 14:6 ('the everlasting euangelion'). When you trace a common Greek word like this in Step 4 of a word study, sample five to ten strategic verses rather than reading all 130.

mc.why: Passing the Unit 11 exam unlocks the Course Certificate of Completion (CTSLACertificate.html). With the certificate earned, you complete the capstone word-study assignment and submit it to Wayne. The certificate marks the formal end of the Language Appreciation course; the capstone marks the beginning of a lifetime of word study.
